segments.expected: "Then the sixth is at Saltmere, on their gate mast, or it isn't at all. And it may be that the fifth is too." Orla said it flatly, as one reads off a gauge that has stuck. "I'll write that today, before anybody has time to hurry. I've seen a girl hurry a crossing because a clerk wanted a sixth before a boat. She's a fitter now, and she's never lit a door since."

segments.expected: It came hot, and it came gladly, the way the Ember always came, as though it had been waiting at the top of a stair to be asked down. The struts ran down the backs of her calves and along the soles of her feet in their dull orange, and the three heat-lines across her chest drew tight from the breastbone to the left shoulder, and she went. It was one low bound, six paces, with the frost going by under her in a grey smear and the black posts going by on either hand.

segments.expected: Healer Aske had the hand at seven on Monday morning, under the lamp at the Wren House, with the frost still on the window.
segments.transcript: Hila Ask had the hand at seven on Monday morning, under the lamp at the Wrenhaus, with the frost still on the window.

segments.expected: They were husks. Kiva had seen husks since she was thirteen, and these were like all the others and not like any of them. Each was the height of a tall man, a column of grey stuff like a sack of fine ash stood on end, belted at the middle by a knot as thick as a man's arm. Each stood on three thin legs, set wide, like a milking stool. They had no faces. They had a breath, which came out of them all over, as frost comes off a field at dawn, and wherever the breath touched the cinder it went white.

segments.expected: They stood in a row. Then they stamped.
segments.transcript: They stood in a row, then they stamped.

segments.expected: It was all three of them at once. They lifted their legs together and put them down together, one, with a dry crunch on the cinder, as men put their feet down when they are marching. Then they leaned. All three leaned together a little to the left, toward the race. Two. They came back. Three. They stamped again. Four.

segments.expected: She had known it would be nobody. She had been nobody in the air over an oak floor a month ago, between an Ember and a stance, and it had been as she remembered it: a quarter of a dram going out of her like a breath, and nothing open, and nothing to stand on, and the left hand cold. This was not that. This was nearer.

This was not that. This was Nira.

segments.expected: It was white. It was white to the wrist and a little past, and the skin over the knuckles had the look of a candle end. When she shut the hand, it shut slowly, all of it, the three fingers as well as the two, as though the order had to go a long way to reach them. There was no pain in it. There was simply a great deal of cold, in a place that she was used to listening to, and the listening had stopped.

segments.expected: It was Wilf Marten who went first, because he had a chair to push and was used to being first. Twenty-Eight's captain declared his four by role and by door. Selka Dray was in it, on two sticks, standing; she was the blade, and she declared her own door herself before Marten could, and he let her. Then Old Four, in Lowen Brask's flat voice, though Brask was not its captain and said so. Then Halden License, by Pettit, who was.

segments.expected: She went down the steps, alone, and walked across the cinder between the two stamping husks as though they were cows in a lane, and picked up the sealed bag by its neck, and walked back. Neither husk turned its head. Kiva did not breathe until the Marshal was on the bottom step again.

segments.expected: "It's not me," she said. "I'll say that first so that it's said. I can't count a thing that keeps time; I've two fingers that tell me it's there, and on a floor they'll tell me about my own heart as soon as anything else. And I'm on the cloth. A catcher's on her knees at a hem with her hands full and her eyes on a heap; you all saw where my eyes were when the first one fell." She looked at the sheet. "It can't be Jude. He's cutting. He has to be looking at a knot, not counting feet."
